/MONDAY THROUGH FRIDAY/...
Issued at 340 AM MDT Sat Oct 31 2026

The approaching storm system continues to look rather messy. 
Multiple competing upper level lows will make for a muddy forcing 
picture across the region. A deep primary trough will be making its 
way across the western CONUS while a moisture laden upper level low 
riding the sub-tropical jet races in around it. The primary 700-mb 
low and the secondary center associated with the subtropical system 
will both pass through the area Sunday evening, leading to drier 
conditions over much of the area Monday morning. After passing our 
area, these two should consolidate into one system and stack on top 
of a rapidly developing surface cyclone. This should take over 
around daybreak Monday, setting up a strong pressure gradient over 
the High Plains and leading to increasing northwest winds Monday 
morning. Widespread gusty northwest winds can be expected Monday 
into Monday night over the High Plains. Confidence remains high in 
fairly widespread gusts of 45 to 55 mph, with still some potential 
to exceed High Wind criteria. Probabilities are generally around 30 
to 40% for all along and east of the Laramie range, including the 
wind prone areas around the I-80 summit and I-25 between Wheatland 
and Glendo. The wind direction is not very favorable for high winds 
at Bordeaux. The lack of vertically stacked westerlies and potential 
for synoptic ascent rather than descent as surface winds increase 
decreases confidence in widespread high winds. 

Forcing will not really favor much lift during this period Monday 
AM, so expect fairly limited coverage around dawn, but this should 
change as the day progresses. Model guidance is now in fairly good 
agreement showing the mid-level low pressure elongating back to
the southeast after it passes through our area. This will be 
forced by lee cyclogenesis ahead of the the primary upper level 
low swinging over the Four Corners which begins to slow down as 
it ejects to the east. This appears to be a very complex 
evolution, but the end result is to turn the wind direction in 
the 700 to 500-mb layer from northwest Monday morning to north 
or even northeast by Monday afternoon. Despite surface downslope
northwesterly winds continuing, we may see support for ascent 
just above the surface layer. Where northwest flow is not as 
unfavorable (Douglas to Chadron corridor), seeing an increase in
appreciable rainfall is more promising. The surface downslope 
will be tough to overcome around the Cheyenne to Sidney 
corridor. Thus, we appear to be finally converging on the 
scenario with moderate precipitation in our northern zones, and 
more limited precipitation further south. 

The latest QPF probabilities reflect the increasing confidence in 
this scenario. LREF probabilities for 0.5" or more of liquid 
precipitation are around 50 to 60% in Rawlins, Douglas, and Chadron, 
which look like the most favorable areas at this time, though it is 
worth mentioning that at least for Rawlins some of this will come 
from the first phase Sunday and Sunday night, with a break early 
Monday morning, and then another round Monday late morning into the 
evening. Precipitation evolution may take on the character of 
typical northerly flow events across our area, with the subtle 
terrain features of the High Plains becoming unusually prominent.
Specifically, look for more precipitation along the north sides
of the Pine Ridge and Cheyenne ridge, with lower totals into 
the Wheatland to Bridgeport corridor and I-80 corridor 
(including Cheyenne) and points southward. Laramie and the I-80
summit will be an area to watch for greater uncertainty. This 
is a pretty unusual synoptic setup with veering winds above 
surface northwest winds, but that surface direction is favorable
for increased precipitation around the city of Laramie.

The last piece of the puzzle with this storm system will be snow 
levels. Snow levels will be fairly high for most of the event, 
especially during the first phase where rain may fall as high as 9 
to 10 kft. However, we can expect gradual advection of colder air 
during the day on Monday to reduce snow levels. By sunset, 700-mb 
temperatures should be below 0C over most of southeast Wyoming. As 
precipitation picks back up midday Monday into the evening, rain may 
change over to snow between 5000 ft and 8000 ft. The precise snow 
level will probably depend on the precipitation rates, with areas of 
heavier precipitation changing over faster, while lighter rates stay 
as rain. The problem with this is that there is considerable high 
end boom scenario potential on snow accumulation if a given area 
flips over faster than expected. The primary areas to watch right
